claims.text: The starting material is a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colony microstructure.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittle behavior.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal lamellar boundaries cause local stress concentrations and contribute to the untreated alloy's brittleness.
A low-level addition of a boron-like element during melting and casting is the proposed intervention.
The added boron-like element will segregate to internal lamellar interfaces.
Segregation of the boron-like element will form enriched interfacial films at lamellar boundaries.
Interfacial segregation will modify the chemistry of the lamellar boundaries.
Modified interfacial chemistry will reduce mechanical-property mismatches across the interfaces.
Modified interfacial chemistry will promote smoother dislocation transmission across lamellar interfaces.
Smoother dislocation transmission will alleviate dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries.
Alleviating dislocation pile-ups will reduce local stress concentrations.
Reduced local stress concentrations will delay microcrack nucleation.
The microalloyed material will have greater elongation to failure than the untreated material at room temperature.
The microalloyed material will maintain or slightly increase yield strength relative to the untreated material.
The microalloyed material will maintain or slightly increase ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated material.
The proposed benefit requires segregation to occur without unwanted phase transformations or coarsening of the lamellar structure.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to room-temperature, quasi-static tensile loading.
